passage: Dear Preeti, I have to write it down. Our project team has five people, and one of them, Vivek, has done almost nothing for three weeks. Vivek is also my friend, the one who covered for me when Mum was ill. So when Jyoti asked in the meeting, "Has everyone finished their part?" I looked at my notes and said nothing. So did Dev and Sara. We all know. Jyoti is now doing double, and yesterday Jyoti stopped smiling at us. The trust in the team feels thinner every day. I am writing to ask you: how do I speak to Vivek without ending the friendship? — Sunaina

qa.q: How long has Vivek done almost nothing for the project?
qa.a: Vivek has done almost nothing for three weeks.

qa.q: Why did Sunaina look at the notes and say nothing when Jyoti asked?
qa.a: Sunaina wanted to protect the friendship with Vivek, who once covered for Sunaina; the silence came from loyalty mixed with guilt.

qa.q: What could Sunaina do before writing off the friendship or the team?
qa.a: Sunaina could talk to Vivek privately and kindly, ask what is going on, and then raise the shared workload openly with the team.

qa.q: How might Jyoti feel doing double and no longer smiling at the others?
qa.a: Jyoti probably feels overloaded and let down, and the loss of smiles suggests the unfairness is starting to turn into resentment.

grounding: Team members see one member not pulling their weight and stay silent to protect the relationship, and the unfairness slowly damages trust.

passage: Payal, can I tell you something I am not proud of? I am Jeevan, remember, the one who said everything was "fine". In our final-year team Arjun did hardly any of the lab reports. Everybody knew. But Arjun is the guy who brought all of us tiffin when we were stuck in the lab till midnight, so nobody wanted to be the one to say it. Meena did Arjun's share twice. I saw her face fall each time and said nothing. Six weeks in, the four of us barely spoke at lunch, and the tension was so thick you could cut it. It was not fine, and I knew.

qa.q: How many times did Meena do Arjun's share?
qa.a: Meena did Arjun's share twice.

qa.q: Why did nobody want to say anything about Arjun's missing work?
qa.a: They liked Arjun for bringing tiffin during late nights and feared spoiling the friendship; loyalty and awkwardness kept the group silent.

qa.q: What could Jeevan have done the first time Meena's face fell?
qa.a: Jeevan could have checked with Meena privately, then raised the imbalance kindly with Arjun, before the silence grew into tension.

qa.q: What might Meena have been feeling when doing Arjun's share and no one spoke up?
qa.a: Meena probably felt tired, unappreciated and a bit invisible; the fallen face shows hurt at the silence of the others.

grounding: Team members see one member not pulling their weight and stay silent to protect the relationship, and the unfairness slowly damages the team's trust.

passage:
I was on the college fest decoration team with Sachin and Vikas. I'll tell you what I saw, though I can't say what Sachin was thinking.
Vikas and Sachin had been friends since school. Every evening the rest of us painted banners while Vikas was “getting supplies,” which meant chai with his girlfriend. Sachin would say, “He's coming, yaar,” and quietly paint Vikas's banner too.
None of us said anything. Vikas was fun, and we didn't want to hurt Sachin's friendship either.
By the second week, the atmosphere changed. People stopped sharing snacks. Two girls quit. When Sachin asked for help with the stage, nobody offered.
On fest day, the banners were up. But I noticed the team never went out together again.

qa.q: What did Vikas say he was doing every evening?
qa.a: He said he was "getting supplies".

qa.q: What might Sachin have been feeling as he painted Vikas's banner too?
qa.a: Sachin may have felt torn and protective, loyal to a friend but probably tired and uneasy about the unfairness.

qa.q: What could the team have done to deal with Vikas fairly?
qa.a: One of them, maybe Sachin, could have spoken to Vikas privately and early, so the problem didn't sour the whole team.

qa.q: How did the silence affect the rest of the team?
qa.a: Trust wore down: people stopped sharing snacks, two quit, and nobody offered Sachin help.

grounding: A teammate describes a team staying silent about a friend's free riding to protect the friendship, and trust slowly souring.

passage:
Week one: The hackathon team had five people. Salma, Kunal's closest friend, said she'd build the login page. Kunal saw her playing games during the work sessions. He said nothing. She's going through a lot, he told himself.
Week two: The others noticed. Deepa asked Kunal, “Is Salma doing anything?” Kunal said, “She'll catch up.” Then he stayed up and built the login page himself.
Week three: The team stopped chatting in the group. Deepa and Arjun started working on their own laptops, not sharing code. When Kunal suggested a team dinner after the demo, nobody answered.
Kunal realised protecting Salma had cost him the team.

qa.q: What did Salma say she would build?
qa.a: She said she'd build the login page.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel as the team went silent in week three?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and regretful, realising that protecting Salma had cost the team's trust.

qa.q: What would you advise Kunal to have done in week one?
qa.a: Kunal could have spoken to Salma privately and asked what was going on, instead of covering for her quietly.

qa.q: How might Deepa have felt when Kunal said "She'll catch up"?
qa.a: Deepa may have felt frustrated and brushed off, sensing that friendship mattered more than fairness.

grounding: Shows a team member protecting a free-riding friend with silence, and the unfairness slowly damaging the team's trust.

passage:
Zubin, you asked about your friend who never does his share at college. Let me tell you about my band. This is your Trisha aunty, and I was twenty.
There were four of us. My best friend Nandini was on keyboard. She kept missing rehearsals: exams, headaches, family things. The rest of us learned her parts on guitar. I kept saying, “She'll come, she'll come,” because I couldn't bear to lose her.
The drummer, Ashok, got quieter. The bassist, Farhan, started coming late too. Why should I try, he said once, if she doesn't have to?
By the college finals, we didn't trust each other at all. We played badly and broke up a month later.
I should have spoken to Nandini, kindly, in the first week.

qa.q: What instrument did Nandini play?
qa.a: Nandini played keyboard.

qa.q: How did young Trisha feel about losing Nandini?
qa.a: She felt afraid and protective, unable to bear losing her best friend, so she kept making excuses.

qa.q: What turning point does Trisha wish had happened in the story?
qa.a: She wishes she had spoken to Nandini kindly in the first week, before the unfairness spread to the rest of the band.

qa.q: How might Farhan have felt about the unfairness?
qa.a: He felt resentful and let down, asking why he should try if Nandini didn't have to.

grounding: An elder recalls staying silent about a friend's free riding in a band to protect the friendship, and the band's trust breaking down.

passage:
With the design submission two days away and Mehul home with fever, the four of them were already short of hands. At 10 p.m. Binita looked around the studio: Ananya cutting foam board, Kiran fixing the model's roof, and Pankaj on the sofa, laptop open to the same slide he'd opened at six. "Almost done with the render," he said. He'd said that yesterday too.
Nobody answered. Pankaj had been their friend since first year; he'd sat with Kiran through a whole night at the hospital once. Calling him out felt like kicking someone who had helped you.
Binita watched Ananya slice the board harder than needed. Kiran didn't look up. At midnight Ananya muttered, "Some of us are doing a four-person job," to no one in particular. Pankaj laughed as if it were a joke. Kiran's jaw tightened. The model would get finished, Binita thought, but something in the group was starting to crack.

qa.q: Who was home with fever?
qa.a: Mehul was home with fever.

qa.q: How does Binita feel watching the silent studio?
qa.a: Binita feels uneasy and torn: Pankaj is a loyal old friend, but the unfairness is clearly straining the others.

qa.q: How could the group raise it without attacking the friendship?
qa.a: One of them, perhaps Binita, could talk to Pankaj privately, say what is missing and ask what is going on before resentment grows.

qa.q: What is the night like for Ananya?
qa.a: Ananya is frustrated and resentful, slicing the board hard and finally muttering about a four-person job.

grounding: Shows team members staying silent about a friend who is not pulling his weight, while the unfairness slowly erodes trust.
